concepts.title: Balance needs three senses and a brain
concepts.body: Balance combines **vision**, **vestibular** (inner ear) and **somatosensory** (feet and joints) input, organised by the brain and executed by strong, quick muscles. A test that removes one input shows which system the person depends on.
concepts.ur: Balance teen systems par chalta hai — vision, inner ear (vestibular) aur feet/joints ki sensation — aur brain in sab ko combine kar ke muscles se kaam leta hai.

concepts.title: Why falls matter
concepts.body: About **one in three adults over 65 falls each year**, and falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of independence. Screening finds people at risk early — and balance training reduces falls.
bullets: Ask: fallen in the past year? Feel unsteady? Worried about falling?
If yes → test (TUG, 30-s chair stand, 4-stage balance test)
concepts.ur: Falls bohat aam hain: 65 saal se upar har teen mein se ek insaan saal mein ek baar girta hai, aur girna chot aur khud-mukhtari khone ki bari wajah hai. Isliye pehle screening karein — “pichhle saal gira? Chalte hue unsteady lagta hai? Girne se dar lagta hai?” Agar jawab haan ho to TUG, 30-s chair stand aur 4-stage balance test karwayein. Balance training se falls kam hotay hain, yeh evidence-based hai.

concepts.title: The 4-stage balance test (STEADI)
concepts.body: Hold each stance for **10 seconds** without support: feet side by side → semi-tandem → tandem (heel to toe) → one leg. **Unable to hold tandem stance for 10 s = increased fall risk.**
concepts.ur: STEADI ka 4-stage test: har stance 10 seconds bina sahare hold karwayein — feet side by side, phir semi-tandem, phir tandem (heel-to-toe), phir ek taang. Agar patient tandem stance 10 s tak hold nahi kar sakta to girne ka khatra barh jata hai. Chhota sa test hai lekin bohat kaam ka.

concepts.title: Make results trustworthy
concepts.body: Most variation between testers comes from the set-up, not the patient.
bullets: Same chair height (about 43–46 cm), footwear and walking aid every time
Read the instructions word for word
Use a gait belt and guard on the weaker side
Record conditions: aid, orthosis, time of day, medication (e.g. 'on' phase in Parkinson's)
concepts.ur: Result tabhi bharosay ke qabil hai jab setup har baar ek jaisa ho. Zyada tar farq tester ke setup se aata hai, patient se nahi. Chair ki height same (43–46 cm), same footwear aur same walking aid. Instructions lafz ba lafz parhein. Weak side par gait belt aur guard rakhein. Aur sab kuch record karein — aid, orthosis, waqt, dawai (Parkinson’s mein “on” phase).

concepts.title: Choose the right test
concepts.body: Match the test to the question you are asking.
concepts.ur: Test sawal ke mutabiq chunein. Ek hi test sab kuch nahi batata: kisi ko fall-risk screening chahiye, kisi ko treatment ke baad progress ka measure, aur kisi ko batana hai ke kaun sa balance system fail ho raha hai. Pehle apna sawal tay karein, phir uske hisaab se test select karein.

concepts.title: Cut-off, MDC and MCID
concepts.body: A **cut-off** flags risk. The **minimal detectable change (MDC)** is the smallest change beyond measurement error. The **minimal clinically important difference (MCID)** is the smallest change that matters to patients.
concepts.ur: Teen alag cheezein hain: cut-off sirf risk flag karta hai. MDC (minimal detectable change) woh sab se chhota change hai jo measurement error se bara ho. MCID (minimal clinically important difference) woh sab se chhota change hai jo patient ke liye mayne rakhta hai. Report karte waqt in teeno ko mix na karein.

concepts.title: Ceiling and floor effects
concepts.body: A test with a **ceiling effect** can't show improvement in people who already score near the top (e.g. Berg in active adults). A **floor effect** hides change in very impaired patients. Pick a test whose range fits the patient.
concepts.ur: Ceiling effect ka matlab: agar patient pehle se top ke qareeb score kar raha ho to test improvement dikha hi nahi sakta (maslan active adults mein Berg). Floor effect mein bohat kamzor patients ki tabdeeli nazar nahi aati. Isliye aisa test chunein jis ki range patient par fit ho.

concepts.title: From score to system
concepts.body: Use the pattern, not just the total. Mini-BESTest sections (anticipatory, reactive, sensory, gait) and mCTSIB conditions show **which system fails** — so training targets it: reactive stepping drills, foam/eyes-closed work, gait with head turns, or strength.
concepts.ur: Sirf total score na dekhein, pattern dekhein. Mini-BESTest ke sections (anticipatory, reactive, sensory, gait) aur mCTSIB ki conditions batati hain ke kaun sa system fail ho raha hai — phir training wahi target karein: reactive stepping drills, foam par aankhein band, head turns ke saath gait, ya strength.

concepts.title: A falls-prevention plan
concepts.body: Falls are multifactorial — treat every factor you find.
bullets: Progressive balance + strength training (e.g. Otago), about 3 hours a week
Review medicines, vision, footwear and home hazards
Check orthostatic blood pressure and continence
Refer unexplained falls, blackouts (syncope) or new neurological signs to a doctor
concepts.ur: Falls multifactorial hotay hain — jo jo factor milay, sab ka ilaaj karein. Progressive balance + strength training (maslan Otago, haftay mein takriban 3 ghantay), dawaiyon, nazar, footwear aur ghar ke hazards ka review, orthostatic BP aur continence check. Unexplained falls, blackouts (syncope) ya naye neurological signs doctor ko refer karein.

The middle 6 metres

Restart from zero
Abandon the test

Use the examiner's arm
Run

No further testing
FGA or Mini-BESTest — fewer ceiling effects

A decline
Not interpretable
Within measurement error

Normal

cards.back: How far a person can lean forward beyond arm's length without stepping (forward stability limit)

cards.front: How is the Functional Reach Test performed?
cards.back: Standing side-on to a wall ruler, arm raised to 90° with a fist, reach forward as far as possible without stepping; measure knuckle movement

cards.front: How is the Functional Reach Test scored?
cards.back: Maximum forward reach in cm (average of 2–3 trials)

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Functional Reach Test?
cards.back: Below 15 cm ≈ 4× fall risk; 15–25 cm ≈ 2× fall risk in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Functional Reach Test best suited to?
cards.back: Older adults; a seated version suits wheelchair users and spinal cord injury

cards.front: What does the Single-leg stance test measure?
cards.back: Static balance on one leg

cards.front: How is the Single-leg stance test performed?
cards.back: Arms crossed, stand on one leg with the other foot off the floor (eyes open, then closed); stop when the foot touches down or the stance foot moves

cards.front: How is the Single-leg stance test scored?
cards.back: Seconds held on one leg (usually up to 30–45 s), best of 3

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Single-leg stance test?
cards.back: Under 5 s = increased risk of injurious falls in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Single-leg stance test best suited to?
cards.back: Quick screen in older adults; ankle sprain and return-to-sport testing (eyes closed)

cards.front: What does the Romberg test measure?
cards.back: Whether standing balance depends on vision — a test of proprioception (dorsal columns)

cards.front: How is the Romberg test performed?
cards.back: Feet together, arms by the sides, 30 s with eyes open then 30 s with eyes closed; guard closely

cards.front: How is the Romberg test scored?
cards.back: Positive if balance is lost with eyes closed but not with eyes open

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Romberg test?
cards.back: Falls only with eyes closed = sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia; unsteady even with eyes open = cerebellar or vestibular problem

cards.front: Which patients is the Romberg test best suited to?
cards.back: Neurological examination — neuropathy, B12 deficiency, dorsal column disease

cards.front: What does the 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed) measure?
cards.back: Gait speed — often called the 'sixth vital sign'

cards.front: How is the 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed) performed?
cards.back: Walk 10 m at comfortable (or fast) speed; time only the middle 6 m to exclude acceleration and deceleration

cards.front: How is the 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed) scored?
cards.back: Gait speed in m/s (6 m ÷ time)

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed)?
cards.back: Stroke: below 0.4 m/s household, 0.4–0.8 limited community, above 0.8 community walker; below 1.0 m/s flags risk in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed) best suited to?
cards.back: Almost every population — stroke, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's, older adults

cards.front: What does the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) measure?
cards.back: Submaximal functional exercise capacity

cards.front: How is the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) performed?
cards.back: Walk as far as possible in 6 minutes up and down a 30 m corridor with standard encouragement each minute; rests allowed, clock keeps running

cards.front: How is the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) scored?
cards.back: Total distance walked in metres (record rests, SpO₂ and Borg scores)

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)?
cards.back: Healthy adults roughly 400–700 m; a change of about 30 m is clinically important in chronic lung disease

cards.front: Which patients is the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) best suited to?
cards.back: COPD, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation

cards.front: What does the Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) measure?
cards.back: Balance while walking under changing demands — speed, head turns, obstacles, stairs

cards.front: How is the Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) performed?
cards.back: 8 walking tasks: level walking, speed changes, horizontal and vertical head turns, pivot turn, stepping over and around obstacles, stairs

cards.front: How is the Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) scored?
cards.back: 8 items scored 0–3; maximum 24

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Dynamic Gait Index (DGI)?
cards.back: 19/24 or less = increased fall risk

cards.front: Which patients is the Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) best suited to?
cards.back: Vestibular disorders, older adults and multiple sclerosis

cards.front: What does the Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) measure?
cards.back: Postural stability during demanding walking tasks, including eyes closed and backwards

cards.front: How is the Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) performed?
cards.back: 10 items: the DGI tasks without 'around obstacles', plus narrow-base (tandem) walking, walking with eyes closed and walking backwards

cards.front: How is the Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) scored?
cards.back: 10 items scored 0–3; maximum 30

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Functional Gait Assessment (FGA)?
cards.back: 22/30 or less = increased fall risk in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) best suited to?
cards.back: Vestibular disorders, Parkinson's, stroke and higher-functioning older adults

cards.front: What does the Mini-BESTest measure?
cards.back: Dynamic balance across four systems — anticipatory, reactive, sensory orientation and gait

cards.front: How is the Mini-BESTest performed?
cards.back: 14 tasks including rising on toes, compensatory stepping after release from a lean, foam stance with eyes closed and a dual-task TUG

cards.front: How is the Mini-BESTest scored?
cards.back: 14 items scored 0–2; maximum 28

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Mini-BESTest?
cards.back: Cut-offs vary by condition — around 19–20/28 for fall risk in Parkinson's and older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Mini-BESTest best suited to?
cards.back: Parkinson's, stroke and vestibular disorders — and to choose which balance system to train

cards.front: What does the Four Square Step Test (FSST) measure?
cards.back: Rapid stepping in all directions over low obstacles

cards.front: How is the Four Square Step Test (FSST) performed?
cards.back: Step through 4 squares made by 4 canes on the floor, clockwise then anticlockwise, facing forward throughout

cards.front: How is the Four Square Step Test (FSST) scored?
cards.back: Seconds to complete the stepping sequence (best of 2 trials)

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Four Square Step Test (FSST)?
cards.back: More than 15 s = increased fall risk in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Four Square Step Test (FSST) best suited to?
cards.back: Older adults, vestibular disorders, stroke and Parkinson's

cards.front: What does the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) measure?
cards.back: Balance and gait together in frail older adults

cards.front: How is the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) performed?
cards.back: Balance items (sitting, rising, standing, nudge, eyes closed, turning 360°, sitting down), then observed gait items

cards.front: How is the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scored?
cards.back: Balance 16 + gait 12 = maximum 28

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA)?
cards.back: 18 or less = high fall risk; 19–23 moderate; 24 or more low

cards.front: Which patients is the Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) best suited to?
cards.back: Frail older adults in residential and acute care

cards.front: What does the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale measure?
cards.back: Balance confidence (fear of falling) during daily activities

cards.front: How is the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale performed?
cards.back: The patient rates their confidence of not losing balance in 16 activities

cards.front: How is the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale scored?
cards.back: Mean confidence 0–100% across 16 activities

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale?
cards.back: Below 67% = increased fall risk in older adults

cards.front: Which patients is the Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale best suited to?
cards.back: Older adults, vestibular disorders, Parkinson's and lower-limb amputees

cards.front: What does the Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation) measure?
cards.back: Which senses (vision, somatosensation, vestibular) a person relies on for standing balance

cards.front: How is the Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation) performed?
cards.back: Stand feet together for 30 s in 4 conditions: firm surface eyes open, firm eyes closed, foam eyes open, foam eyes closed

cards.front: How is the Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation) scored?
cards.back: Seconds (up to 30) held in each of the 4 conditions, with sway noted

cards.front: Key cut-off or interpretation for the Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation)?
cards.back: Losing balance only on foam with eyes closed = poor use of vestibular input; losing it on a firm surface with eyes closed = somatosensory loss

cards.front: Which patients is the Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation) best suited to?
cards.back: Dizziness and vestibular rehabilitation, neuropathy and older adults

cards.front: Which three senses does balance rely on?
cards.back: Vision, vestibular and somatosensory. Eyes, inner ear, and feet/joints.

cards.front: Which test times standing up, walking 3 m, turning and sitting?
cards.back: Timed Up and Go. TUG = up, 3 m, turn, back, sit.

cards.front: Which test measures gait speed?
cards.back: 10-Metre Walk Test. Time over the middle 6 m → m/s.

cards.front: Which test measures fear of falling / balance confidence?
cards.back: ABC scale. Activities-specific Balance Confidence scale.

cards.front: Which test measures submaximal exercise capacity?
cards.back: 6-Minute Walk Test. Distance in 6 minutes reflects endurance.

cards.front: About how many adults over 65 fall each year?
cards.back: About 1 in 3. Roughly a third — screening matters.

cards.front: Which test shows whether balance depends on vision?
cards.back: Romberg test. Compare eyes open vs eyes closed.

cards.front: Which test measures how far you can lean forward without stepping?
cards.back: Functional Reach Test. Forward stability limit.

cards.front: In the 4-stage balance test, each stance is held for…
cards.back: 10 seconds. 10 s per stage; failing tandem stance = fall risk.

cards.front: Which test counts sit-to-stands in a fixed time?
cards.back: 30-Second Chair Stand. 30-s CST counts stands; 5xSTS times five stands.

cards.front: Which test times walking speed over a short distance?
cards.back: 10-Metre Walk Test. Gait speed (m/s) — the 'sixth vital sign'.

cards.front: Before any balance test you should…
cards.back: Guard closely (gait belt) and clear the area. Safety first — stand close on the weaker side.

cards.front: Which scale scores 14 everyday balance tasks out of 56?
cards.back: Berg Balance Scale. Berg: 14 items × 4 = 56.

cards.front: In the 10-metre walk test you time…
cards.back: The middle 6 metres. Excluding acceleration and deceleration.

cards.front: During the 6MWT the patient needs to rest. You…
cards.back: Let them rest while the clock keeps running. Rests are allowed; time continues (ATS).

cards.front: In the TUG the patient may…
cards.back: Use their usual walking aid. Usual aid is allowed — record it.

cards.front: An active 60-year-old scores 56/56 on the Berg but reports near-falls. Next test?
cards.back: FGA or Mini-BESTest — fewer ceiling effects. The Berg has a ceiling; harder tests reveal deficits.

cards.front: Gait speed improves from 0.62 to 0.75 m/s after 6 weeks. This is…
cards.back: A clinically meaningful change (> 0.1 m/s). ≈ 0.1 m/s is the MCID.

cards.front: Unsteady even with eyes open on the Romberg suggests…
cards.back: A cerebellar or vestibular problem rather than proprioceptive loss. Romberg is only 'positive' when vision was compensating.

cards.front: A 78-year-old: TUG 16 s, cannot hold tandem stance for 10 s, one fall last month, on three blood-pressure tablets. — Best plan?
cards.back: Multifactorial: progressive strength/balance programme, orthostatic BP check and medicine review. Several risk factors — treat all of them.

cards.front: mCTSIB: stable in conditions 1–3, falls within 6 s on foam with eyes closed. — Interpretation and training?
cards.back: Poor use of vestibular input — foam/eyes-closed and head-movement balance training. Only vestibular input remains in condition 4.

cards.front: Parkinson's: TUG 11 s alone, 19 s while counting backwards by 3s. — What does this show?
cards.back: Dual-task interference — a fall-risk factor; train walking with cognitive tasks. A large dual-task cost predicts falls.

cards.front: Stroke patient: gait speed 0.35 m/s. — What level of walking does this predict?
cards.back: Household walking. < 0.4 m/s = household ambulator (Perry).

cards.front: COPD rehab: 6MWT 320 m at baseline, 345 m at 8 weeks. — Interpretation?
cards.back: Clinically important improvement (≈ 25–30 m MCID). A change of about 25–30 m or more is meaningful in COPD.

cards.front: An older adult avoids going out since a fall; ABC 52%, Berg 49/56. — Main problem to address?
cards.back: Fear of falling and activity restriction — graded exposure plus balance training. Confidence is far lower than measured balance.

cards.front: Recurrent falls 'out of nowhere' with brief loss of consciousness. — Best action?
cards.back: Medical referral for possible syncope (cardiac/neurological) before balance training. Falls with blackouts need medical work-up first.

cards.front: Peripheral neuropathy: fine with eyes open; sways and steps with eyes closed on a firm floor. — Best home advice?
cards.back: Night lights and visual compensation, plus proprioceptive balance training. Sensory ataxia: support vision and train the remaining systems.

cards.front: Which training has the strongest evidence for preventing falls in older adults?
cards.back: Progressive balance and functional strength training, about 3 hours a week. Challenging balance + strength, enough dose (e.g. Otago).

cards.front: Mini-BESTest: lowest scores in the reactive-postural-control section. — Training priority?
cards.back: Compensatory stepping (perturbation) training. Train the failing system — reactive stepping.

cards.front: Berg Balance Scale — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Minimal detectable change is about 5–7 points. In high-functioning people it hits the ceiling — use the FGA or Mini-BESTest.

cards.front: Timed Up and Go (TUG) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Add a cognitive task (TUG-cognitive, e.g. counting back by 3s): a large slowdown flags dual-task fall risk.

cards.front: Five Times Sit-to-Stand (5xSTS) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Note the strategy too: pushing with the hands, a wide stance or losing balance adds information beyond the time.

cards.front: 30-Second Chair Stand — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: If the patient must push up with the arms, the score is 0 — record it and use the 5xSTS or a modified version instead.

cards.front: Functional Reach Test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Watch the strategy: reaching by trunk flexion and a hip strategy is different from simply protracting the scapula.

cards.front: Single-leg stance test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Values fall with age — most adults under 60 manage 30 s or more with eyes open.

cards.front: Romberg test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Stand close with arms ready. The sharpened (tandem) Romberg is more sensitive in mild deficits.

cards.front: 10-Metre Walk Test (gait speed) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A change of about 0.1 m/s is clinically meaningful; gait speed predicts falls, hospital admission and survival.

cards.front: Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Follow the ATS protocol exactly — encouragement and track length change the result. Stop for chest pain, severe breathlessness or marked desaturation.

cards.front: Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Ceiling effect in mild deficits — the FGA adds harder items (tandem walking, eyes closed, walking backwards).

cards.front: Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Fewer ceiling effects than the DGI or Berg — a good choice for active patients.

cards.front: Mini-BESTest — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Unlike the Berg it tests reactive stepping responses, which matter most for preventing falls.

cards.front: Four Square Step Test (FSST) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Stepping sideways and backwards over obstacles mirrors real-life fall situations.

cards.front: Tinetti Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Quick and observational, but less sensitive in higher-functioning people.

cards.front: Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) scale — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Low confidence restricts activity and leads to deconditioning — treat fear of falling, not only balance.

cards.front: Modified CTSIB (sensory organisation) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Use the failing condition to choose training — e.g. foam and eyes-closed practice when vestibular input is under-used.
